subject: Art & Design
title: The Color Wheel: How It All Connects
description: Learn The Color Wheel: How It All Connects in one minute.

hook.text: Isaac Newton split white light through a prism and arranged the resulting colors in a circle.

buildup.text: The color wheel organizes hues by their relationship: primaries, secondaries, and tertiaries.

discovery.text: Colors opposite each other on the wheel — like red and green — create maximum visual contrast.

twist.text: There's no single 'correct' wheel. Painters, printers, and screens each use different primaries.

climax.text: RYB for paint, CMYK for print, RGB for screens — three wheels for three different worlds.

punchline.text: One circle organizes every color you'll ever use.

quiz.question: Why are there different color wheel models?
options: Different media (paint, print, screen) mix color differently
Scientists can't agree on primary colors

details.summary: The color wheel, first developed by Isaac Newton in 1666, organizes colors in a circle showing relationships between primary, secondary, and tertiary colors. It remains the foundational tool for understanding color harmony, mixing, and contrast in art, design, fashion, and digital media.
details.whyItMatters: Every color decision in design — whether choosing a brand palette or painting a room — relies on relationships the color wheel reveals.
takeaways: Newton created the first color wheel in 1666
Organizes primary, secondary, and tertiary color relationships
Foundation for understanding harmony, mixing, and contrast

faq.question: Why is the color wheel arranged in a circle?
faq.answer: The circle represents the continuous spectrum of visible light bent back on itself, connecting red and violet. This arrangement reveals complementary colors (opposites), analogous colors (neighbors), and triadic relationships (equidistant points) — relationships invisible in a linear spectrum.

faq.question: Are there different versions of the color wheel?
faq.answer: Yes. The traditional RYB wheel (red-yellow-blue) is used in painting. The RGB wheel (red-green-blue) is used for digital screens. The CMY wheel (cyan-magenta-yellow) is used in printing. Each serves its medium, but the underlying relationships remain consistent.
